messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Threat → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 46-year-old married man who works as a curriculum designer for a public school district, spending much of his week moving between school buildings, observing classrooms, and meeting with teachers about lesson planning. The event he returns to in fragments happened late one afternoon as he was leaving a middle school campus after a meeting. In the parking lot, a police officer stopped him, demanded identification, and escalated quickly when Kwame did not immediately understand why he was being questioned. He remembers the officer’s voice becoming sharper, the sudden command to keep his hands visible, the metallic sound of equipment shifting on the officer’s belt, and the feeling that one wrong movement could get him hurt or killed. What remains most vivid is not a clean sequence of images but the bodily terror of being pinned in place under suspicion while staff and parents moved at a distance, close enough to witness but too far to interrupt. Even now, when he tries to describe it, he loses the thread. He says there are parts he knows happened but “can’t put into words,” as though the experience sits in him more as a surge of fear than as a story.

In the weeks afterward, Kwame did not feel as if the incident had ended. He began moving through the world in a state of heightened watchfulness, scanning parking lots, doorways, and the faces of uniformed officers near schools and public buildings. He noticed himself startling hard at sudden noises—the crackle of a radio, a car door slamming, footsteps approaching too quickly behind him. When something reminded him of the stop, his body reacted before he had time to think: his chest tightened, his shoulders locked, and he felt a rush of heat and dread that made him feel as if he were back in danger. That constant state of being on guard seemed to make the memory even less graspable. When he became keyed up, any attempt to recall what happened left him overwhelmed so fast that he had to stop talking. At times there was no picture at all, only the full emotional force of the moment crashing into him—terror, humiliation, the certainty that he was unsafe—without a clear image attached to it. The more jumpy and watchful he felt, the less able he was to hold the event in words.

This pattern became especially clear in his work. Kwame’s job requires him to enter school campuses, sign in at front offices, and cross parking lots where school resource officers or local police are sometimes present. On those mornings he found himself immediately alert to where every officer was standing, whether anyone was looking at him, how visible his hands were, and how quickly he could produce his badge. If a radio chirped or an officer called out to someone nearby, he would jolt and feel his heart pounding in his throat. Later, colleagues might ask why he had seemed distracted in a planning meeting, and he would want to explain, but the effort to recount the stop would bring such a wave of feeling that he would break off midsentence. He came to dread not only police presence itself but the internal collapse that followed any reminder, because once his body went on high alert the memory stopped being something he could narrate and became something he simply endured.

At home, his wife has seen him become increasingly tense in ordinary moments. If there is unexpected knocking at the door or a siren outside, he reacts instantly, his body braced before he has oriented to what is happening. She has tried to ask him what, exactly, comes back to him, and he often answers with frustration that he does not know how to say it. He may start with one concrete detail—the officer’s tone, the command not to move—only to become flooded and fall silent, pressing his palms into his knees as if to steady himself. What frightens him most is that the danger still feels present in his body even when his mind cannot produce a full scene. He has come to believe that if he lets himself go near the memory, he will be swallowed by it.

By the time he sought help, the strain had begun to alter how he moved through both work and family life. He was taking longer routes across campuses to avoid passing near officers, arriving to meetings already tense from scanning his surroundings, and going home exhausted from maintaining that level of vigilance all day. He finally agreed to therapy after a recent school visit in which a uniformed officer greeted him casually from across a hallway; Kwame startled so violently that he dropped the folders he was carrying and had to lock himself in an empty office bathroom while his body shook. Sitting in the intake, he said he wants to be able to tell what happened without feeling overtaken by it. At the same time, he is afraid that putting the experience into words will make the fear even more real, and that his body will keep reacting as though the next encounter could turn deadly.
